title: Processes, Threads and the OS
summary: How the operating system shares one machine among many programs: kernel vs user space, syscalls, processes, threads, scheduling and virtual memory.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a **process** and a **thread**? Give one situation where you'd prefer each.
questions.hint: Think apartments and roommates: what is private and what is shared?
keyPoints: A process has its own virtual address space, file descriptors and resources; processes are isolated
Threads live inside a process, each with its own stack, registers and program counter, sharing the heap and fds
Threads are cheaper to create and switch, and communicate via shared memory; processes need IPC
A crash or memory corruption in one thread can take down the whole process; a process crash is contained
Example: processes for isolation (browser tabs, separate services), threads for cheap parallel work on shared data

questions.prompt: What is a **system call**, and why can't a normal program just talk to the disk or network card directly? Roughly how expensive is a syscall compared with a function call, and how does that affect how you write I/O code?
questions.hint: The CPU has privilege modes. What would happen if any program could program the disk controller?
keyPoints: The CPU runs user programs in an unprivileged user mode; only the kernel (kernel mode) can access hardware and all memory
A syscall is a controlled switch into the kernel at a trusted entry point to request a service (read, write, open, socket...)
This protects isolation and security: programs can't corrupt each other or the OS
A syscall costs roughly 100 ns to 1 µs vs about 1 ns for a function call
So batch and buffer I/O: one large write instead of many tiny ones

questions.prompt: A WebSocket server works fine in testing, but in production it starts failing around 1,000 concurrent users with `EMFILE: too many open files`. What is happening and how would you fix it?
questions.hint: What does the kernel hand back when a socket is opened?
keyPoints: Every socket (and file) uses a file descriptor; the per-process limit is often 1024 by default (ulimit -n)
~1000 connections plus files, logs and DB connections exhaust the limit, so new accept/open calls fail
Fix: raise the limit (ulimit -n / systemd LimitNOFILE / container settings) to tens or hundreds of thousands
Also check for fd leaks (sockets or files never closed) and use connection pooling for outgoing connections
Mentions monitoring open fd count

questions.prompt: A thread-per-connection server handles 20,000 concurrent connections. Each thread reserves an 8 MB stack but actually touches about 100 KB. The CPU does 40,000 context switches per second at ~5 µs each. Estimate (a) reserved virtual memory, (b) real memory used by stacks, (c) CPU fraction lost to switching.
questions.hint: Multiply, then watch the units: 1 MB = 1,000 KB, 1 s = 1,000,000 µs.
keyPoints: (a) 20,000 × 8 MB = 160 GB of virtual address space (fine on 64-bit, it's only reserved)
(b) 20,000 × 100 KB = 2 GB of actual RAM
(c) 40,000 × 5 µs = 200,000 µs = 0.2 s per second ≈ 20% of one core
Explains virtual vs resident memory: pages get RAM only when touched
Notes that event loops (one thread, many connections) avoid much of this cost

questions.prompt: Explain **virtual memory**. If two processes both have a pointer to address `0x7f001000`, do they see the same data? What is a page fault, and what is the OOM killer?
questions.hint: Each process has its own page table. The MMU translates every address.
keyPoints: Each process sees a private virtual address space; the MMU translates virtual pages (usually 4 KB) to physical frames using per-process page tables
The same virtual address in two processes maps to different physical memory, so they don't see each other's data (unless memory is deliberately shared)
A page fault happens when a page isn't mapped or is not in RAM; the kernel allocates it or loads it (from swap or a file) and resumes
Enables isolation, lazy allocation, swap, and sharing of read-only code
When RAM runs out, Linux's OOM killer kills a process (often the largest); in containers this shows as OOMKilled

questions.prompt: Your team runs a Node.js image-thumbnail API on Kubernetes, one pod per 4-core node. During deploys some uploads fail mid-request, and under load the pods get `OOMKilled`. Design the process/thread layout and shutdown behavior you'd use. Justify each choice using today's concepts.
questions.hint: Think about which work is CPU-bound, how Node uses cores, what signal Kubernetes sends before killing a pod, and what limits memory.
keyPoints: Thumbnailing is CPU-bound; a single Node thread can use one core, so use a worker thread pool (or multiple processes) sized to cores
Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight ones, then exit within the grace period (default 30 s) before SIGKILL
Fix OOM: bound concurrency (queue requests so only N images decode at once), stream instead of buffering whole files, set heap size flags and container memory limits consistently
Mentions that workers share the process's memory limit, so concurrency × per-image memory must fit under the limit
Optionally: readiness probe fails during shutdown so the load balancer stops sending traffic
